# `silk/system/signal_watch`

<!-- Generated by silk doc-reference. Do not edit by hand. -->

Receive process signals, such as an interrupt or a terminal resize, through a descriptor that an
event loop can watch.

## When to use
Use a [`SignalWatch`](#SignalWatch) when a signal must become an event of your loop instead of ending the
process, as for `process.on("SIGINT")` in a JavaScript runtime. Add each signal with
[`SignalWatch.add`](#SignalWatch.impl.add), register [`SignalWatch.descriptor`](#SignalWatch.impl.descriptor) with a reactor, such as
`silk.io.reactor`, for reads, and call [`SignalWatch.read`](#SignalWatch.impl.read) when it is readable.

## Details
While a signal is in the watch, its default action does not happen: the signal only makes the
descriptor readable. [`SignalWatch.remove`](#SignalWatch.impl.remove) and dropping the watch give each signal back its
earlier behavior. A signal that arrives more than one time before a read is reported one time.

The watch uses `signalfd` on Linux and a kqueue with `EVFILT_SIGNAL` filters on Darwin. The
descriptor is nonblocking and close-on-exec.

## Errors
Each operation fails with [`SignalError`](#SignalError): the [`SignalOperation`](#SignalOperation) and the native error code.

## Gotchas
- Keep one watch for each signal in a process. Two watches of one signal take its arrivals
  from each other.
- On Linux, the watch blocks its signals in the thread that adds them, and threads that start
  later inherit the block. Open the watch and add its signals on the main thread before the
  program starts other threads: a thread that started earlier still gets the signal with its
  default action.
- On Darwin, the watch sets a signal whose default action ends or stops the process to be
  ignored while it is in the watch. A child started with `posix_spawn` or `exec` gets that
  ignored setting unless the starter resets it, as `silk.system.subprocess` does.
- `SIGKILL` and `SIGSTOP` cannot be watched.
- The module is empty on targets other than Darwin on x86_64 or aarch64, and Linux with GNU libc
  on x86_64 or aarch64.

## Examples
### Receive a signal that the process sends to itself
```silk
import silk.core.effect { Effect }
import silk.core.result { Result }
import silk.system.signal_watch { SignalError, SignalWatch }

unsafe extern "C" fn getpid() -> i32
unsafe extern "C" fn kill(pid: i32, signal: i32) -> i32

effect fn program() -> i32 ! SignalError {
  let mut watch = run SignalWatch.open()
  // SIGUSR1 ends the process by default; in the watch it only makes the descriptor readable.
  let user = SignalWatch.userOne()
  run watch.add(user)
  if unsafe kill(unsafe getpid(), user) != 0 { return 1 }
  let mut received: [i32; 4] = [0; 4]
  let count = run watch.read(&mut received)
  if count != 1 || received[0] != user { return 1 }
  // Nothing more arrived, so a read does not block and returns 0.
  let more = run watch.read(&mut received)
  if more != 0 { return 1 }
  run watch.remove(user)
  return 0
}

pub effect fn main() -> i32 {
  return match run Effect.result(program()) {
    Result<i32, SignalError>.Success { value } => value
    Result<i32, SignalError>.Failure { .. } => 1
  }
}
```

Import as `SignalWatch` with `import silk.system.signal_watch { SignalWatch }`.

## `SignalError`

```silk
pub struct SignalError
```

A failed [`SignalWatch`](#SignalWatch) operation: which one, and the native error code.

### Details
`code` is the `errno` value of the failed system call, such as 22 (`EINVAL`) for a signal number
that cannot be watched, or 24 (`EMFILE`) when the process has too many open descriptors.

<a id="SignalWatch"></a>

## `SignalWatch`

```silk
pub struct SignalWatch
```

A descriptor that becomes readable when one of its signals arrives.

### Details
While a signal is in the watch, its default action does not happen. The descriptor is
nonblocking and close-on-exec. Dropping the watch removes each of its signals, which gives each
one back its earlier behavior, and closes the descriptor.

### Gotchas
- Keep one watch for each signal in a process.
- On Linux, add signals on the main thread before other threads start. A thread that started
  earlier still gets the signal with its default action.
- On Darwin, a signal whose default action ends or stops the process is set to be ignored while
  it is in the watch, and a child started by `exec` alone inherits that.

<a id="SignalWatch.impl.add"></a>

### Method `add`

```silk
pub effect fn add(self: &mut Self, signal: i32) -> () ! SignalError
```

Adds `signal`: from now on it makes the descriptor readable instead of taking its default
action. Adding a signal that is in the watch does nothing.

#### Errors
[`SignalError`](#SignalError) with operation `Add`, with code 22 (`EINVAL`) for `SIGKILL`, `SIGSTOP`, or a
number that is not a signal of the system: 1 to 64 on Linux, 1 to 31 on Darwin.

<a id="SignalWatch.impl.remove"></a>

### Method `remove`

```silk
pub effect fn remove(self: &mut Self, signal: i32) -> () ! SignalError
```

Removes `signal`, and gives it back its behavior from before [`SignalWatch.add`](#SignalWatch.impl.add). Removing a
signal that is not in the watch does nothing.

#### Details
An arrival of `signal` that was not read yet is discarded.

#### Errors
[`SignalError`](#SignalError) with operation `Remove` if the system refuses the change, or with code 22
(`EINVAL`) for a number that is not a signal of the system.

<a id="SignalWatch.impl.contains"></a>

### Method `contains`

```silk
pub fn contains(self: &Self, signal: i32) -> bool
```

Returns whether `signal` is in the watch.

<a id="SignalWatch.impl.read"></a>

### Method `read`

```silk
pub effect fn read(self: &mut Self, signals: &mut [i32]) -> usize ! SignalError
```

Writes the signals that arrived since the last read to the start of `signals`, and returns
their number. It never blocks: with no arrival, it returns 0.

#### Details
A signal that arrived more than one time is written one time. At most `signals.length`
signals are written; the others stay for the next read.

#### Errors
[`SignalError`](#SignalError) with operation `Read` if the system call fails.
